blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Four functions of the dplyr package choose parts of a data frame. These functions are called verbs, because each does one thing to a data frame. Inside them you name columns without $. None of them changes the data frame it was given. To keep a result, assign it to a name.

select() keeps the columns you name, in the order you name them, and drops the rest. Every row is kept.

rename() changes the names of columns you name, with new_name = old_name, and keeps every column, in its place.

filter() keeps the rows for which a condition is TRUE. A condition is built from comparisons (== equal to, != not equal to, < less than, > greater than, <= at most, >= at least) joined by & (and), | (or) and ! (not). R works out each comparison before it joins them with & or |, so each side of | must be a whole comparison. Several conditions separated by commas must all be TRUE. A row whose condition is NA is dropped. So a test for a missing value is written is.na(x), never x == NA.

arrange() sorts the rows by the values of the columns named, smallest first. desc() sorts largest first. Missing values go to the end either way.

The pipe passes the data frame on its left to the function on its right, as that function’s first argument: x |> f(y) is f(x, y).

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
filter() keeps rows. You write a test, and a row stays only if the test says TRUE for it.

Here is the trap that catches everyone once. A test on a missing value gives neither TRUE nor FALSE. It gives NA, “don’t know”. filter() drops every row where the test says “don’t know”. To find the missing ones, ask is.na(), which answers TRUE or FALSE.

Read each |> as “then”: take the penguins, then keep these rows, then keep these columns, then sort.

blocks.alt: A bar chart with three bars: all rows 344, island is Dream or Torgersen 176, and sex is FEMALE 85.
blocks.caption: Rows left after each filter() step in the search for the heaviest females on Dream and Torgersen: 344 rows in the file, 176 on Dream or Torgersen, and 85 of those with sex recorded as FEMALE. Each condition can only take rows away.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with a question that fails. Which rows have no body mass recorded?

Load the two packages and read the raw file, as the section on reading a raw file showed. show_col_types = FALSE turns off the column report that read_csv() prints, because you have already read it once.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

warn.conflicts = FALSE turns off the masking message that section 6 explained. Every block in this section loads dplyr that way.

The column is called Body Mass (g), with spaces and brackets. A name like that breaks R’s rules for names, so you wrap it in backticks, as the section on tidy data showed. Now write the question the way it sounds in English: keep the rows where body mass equals missing.

penguins_raw |>
  filter(`Body Mass (g)` == NA)
# A tibble: 0 × 17
# ℹ 17 variables: studyName <chr>, Sample Number <dbl>, Species <chr>,
#   Region <chr>, Island <chr>, Stage <chr>, Individual ID <chr>,
#   Clutch Completion <chr>, Date Egg <date>, Culmen Length (mm) <dbl>,
#   Culmen Depth (mm) <dbl>, Flipper Length (mm) <dbl>,
#   Body Mass (g) <dbl>, Sex <chr>, Delta 15 N (o/oo) <dbl>,
#   Delta 13 C (o/oo) <dbl>, Comments <chr>

R says: a tibble with 0 rows. No error, no warning. It would be easy to write down “no row is missing its body mass”.

That is wrong, and here is why. == compares each value with NA. A comparison with an unknown value is itself unknown, so the answer on every row is NA. filter() keeps a row only when the answer is TRUE, and drops it when the answer is NA. So it drops all 344.

Ask the question with is.na() instead. It answers TRUE for a missing value and FALSE for anything else. Keep four columns, so the answer fits on the screen.

penguins_raw |>
  filter(is.na(`Body Mass (g)`)) |>
  select(Species, `Individual ID`, `Body Mass (g)`, Comments)
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  Species                       `Individual ID` `Body Mass (g)` Comments
  <chr>                         <chr>                     <dbl> <chr>
1 Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis a… N2A2                         NA Adult n…
2 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis p… N38A2                        NA Adult n…

Two rows, N2A2 and N38A2. Their Comments column starts “Adult n”, cut short to fit the screen; in the file it reads “Adult not sampled”. The empty answer above was not a finding about the penguins. It was a property of ==.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
is.na() finds what R reads as missing. A missing value written in the file as -99, or as “not recorded”, is not NA unless you told read_csv() about it when you read the file. For such a column is.na() finds nothing, for a different reason, and the section on missing values deals with it.

Newer dplyr (1.2.0) adds filter_out(), which names the rows to drop; its changelog says it is “particularly useful when missing values are involved”. This book’s outputs come from dplyr 1.1.4.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now answer a real question in steps: among the female penguins on Dream and Torgersen islands, which were the heaviest?

First keep the columns you need, and give them names you can type. Inside select(), new_name = old_name renames as it keeps. starts_with("Culmen") keeps both culmen columns (the culmen is the ridge along the top of the bill) without typing either name.

penguins_small <- penguins_raw |>
  select(
    species = Species,
    island = Island,
    sex = Sex,
    body_mass_g = `Body Mass (g)`,
    starts_with("Culmen")
  )

penguins_small
# A tibble: 344 × 6
   species                 island sex   body_mass_g `Culmen Length (mm)`
   <chr>                   <chr>  <chr>       <dbl>                <dbl>
 1 Adelie Penguin (Pygosc… Torge… MALE         3750                 39.1
 2 Adelie Penguin (Pygosc… Torge… FEMA…        3800                 39.5
 3 Adelie Penguin (Pygosc… Torge… FEMA…        3250                 40.3
 4 Adelie Penguin (Pygosc… Torge… <NA>           NA                 NA
 5 Adelie Penguin (Pygosc… Torge… FEMA…        3450                 36.7
 6 Adelie Penguin (Pygosc… Torge… MALE         3650                 39.3
 7 Adelie Penguin (Pygosc… Torge… FEMA…        3625                 38.9
 8 Adelie Penguin (Pygosc… Torge… MALE         4675                 39.2
 9 Adelie Penguin (Pygosc… Torge… <NA>         3475                 34.1
10 Adelie Penguin (Pygosc… Torge… <NA>         4250                 42
# ℹ 334 more rows
# ℹ 1 more variable: `Culmen Depth (mm)` <dbl>

Still 344 rows: select() never drops a row. Six columns. The two culmen columns keep their old names, because starts_with() chose them and nothing renamed them. Long text is cut short to fit the screen: FEMA… is “FEMALE”. A tibble prints a missing text value as <NA>; it is the same NA.

rename() does the renaming without dropping anything. Check that it keeps all 17 columns:

penguins_raw |>
  rename(body_mass_g = `Body Mass (g)`) |>
  ncol()
[1] 17

Now the rows. Keep the two islands with %in%, which asks “is this value one of these?”. Then count the rows with nrow().

penguins_small |>
  filter(island %in% c("Dream", "Torgersen")) |>
  nrow()
[1] 176

Add the second condition after a comma. Both must be TRUE for a row to stay. The file writes sex in capitals, so the test is sex == "FEMALE", not "female".

penguins_small |>
  filter(island %in% c("Dream", "Torgersen"), sex == "FEMALE") |>
  nrow()
[1] 85

Then sort the heaviest first, and look at the top five: print(n = 5) shows only the first 5 rows.

penguins_small |>
  filter(island %in% c("Dream", "Torgersen"), sex == "FEMALE") |>
  arrange(desc(body_mass_g)) |>
  print(n = 5)
# A tibble: 85 × 6
  species                  island sex   body_mass_g `Culmen Length (mm)`
  <chr>                    <chr>  <chr>       <dbl>                <dbl>
1 Chinstrap penguin (Pygo… Dream  FEMA…        4150                 46
2 Chinstrap penguin (Pygo… Dream  FEMA…        3950                 45.2
3 Chinstrap penguin (Pygo… Dream  FEMA…        3900                 47.5
4 Chinstrap penguin (Pygo… Dream  FEMA…        3850                 47.6
5 Adelie Penguin (Pygosce… Torge… FEMA…        3800                 39.5
# ℹ 80 more rows
# ℹ 1 more variable: `Culmen Depth (mm)` <dbl>

The heaviest of those 85 rows has a body mass of 4150 g, a Chinstrap penguin on Dream.

Read the pipe aloud, with “then” for each |>: take the small table, then keep the rows on Dream or Torgersen where sex is FEMALE, then sort by body mass, largest first.

Here is what each step left.

Step Rows left
all rows 344
island is Dream or Torgersen 176
and sex is FEMALE 85

Last, check that none of this changed the raw data.

nrow(penguins_raw)
[1] 344

Still 344. Each verb handed back a new data frame. Only penguins_small was kept, because only it was given a name.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The 85 is a count of rows in this file with “FEMALE” in the sex column. Eleven rows have no sex recorded, and some of them may be female. So 85 is the number of rows with sex recorded as FEMALE on those two islands, not a count of female birds.

The count holds for this file only. It says nothing about how many penguins live on either island.

points.html: The error is to write filter(x == NA) to find missing values. Write filter(is.na(x)).
When a filter returns 0 rows, check the test before you report the zero: print the values you tested against.
filter() drops a row whose test is NA. Whenever you report a count after a filter, say whether missing values were dropped by it.
Never type a filter into the raw file by deleting rows. Write the filter() line in the script.
A verb that is not assigned changes nothing.
Rename awkward column names once, near the top of the script, into snake case (lowercase words joined by _).
filter() keeps the rows that pass the test you wrote. It cannot tell you whether that test matches your question.

blocks.prompt: A first-year resident has ten minutes and a whiteboard. Their code filter(hb == NA) on an anaemia survey file returned no rows, and they have written “no missing haemoglobin values” in their results. Explain what happened and how to check.
blocks.answer:
Write three values on the board: 11.2, NA, 9.8. Under each, write what hb == NA gives: NA, NA, NA. Comparing anything with an unknown value gives an unknown answer, even comparing NA with NA.

Then say what filter() does with the answers. It keeps a row only when the answer is TRUE. It drops FALSE and it drops NA. Every answer was NA, so every row was dropped. The empty result is a property of ==, not of their survey.

Now write is.na(hb) under the same three values: FALSE, TRUE, FALSE. That is a real answer on every row, so filter(is.na(hb)) keeps exactly the rows with no value.

Ask them to run it and report the number it gives. Then ask them to put that number in their results. Ask them to add how many rows the survey had, so a reader can see the denominator.

blocks.prompt: Without looking back, take each of select(), rename(), filter() and arrange() in turn. Say what it does to the rows and to the columns. Then say what it does to the data frame you gave it.
blocks.answer:
select() keeps the columns you name, in that order, and keeps every row. The function rename() changes column names and keeps every row and every column. The function filter() keeps the rows whose condition is TRUE, dropping FALSE and NA, and keeps every column. The function arrange() keeps every row and column and changes only the order of the rows, with missing values last.

None of them changes the data frame you gave it. Each returns a new one, which is lost unless you assign it with <-.

blocks.prompt: Write the first block of your analysis script after the line that reads the penguin file. It should keep the species, island, sex, flipper length and body mass columns, and give each a snake-case name that carries its unit. Show that the result has 344 rows and 5 columns.
blocks.answer:
One answer. Your names may differ; check that each is lowercase, joined by _, and ends in its unit where it has one.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins <- penguins_raw |>
  select(
    species = Species,
    island = Island,
    sex = Sex,
    flipper_length_mm = `Flipper Length (mm)`,
    body_mass_g = `Body Mass (g)`
  )

nrow(penguins)
ncol(penguins)
[1] 344
[1] 5

select() with new_name = old_name keeps and renames in one step. No row is lost, because select() never drops rows. The raw object penguins_raw still has all 17 columns.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up clinic register has three rows. dplyr makes tibble() available too.

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

clinic <- tibble(
  id = c(101, 102, 103),
  sex = c("F", "M", "F"),
  weight_kg = c(61.2, 78.5, NA)
)

Write one line for each. (a) Keep the rows for women. (b) Keep only the id and weight_kg columns, in that order. (c) Sort it heaviest first; before you run it, say where the row with no weight will go.
blocks.answer:
clinic |>
  filter(sex == "F")
# A tibble: 2 × 3
     id sex   weight_kg
  <dbl> <chr>     <dbl>
1   101 F          61.2
2   103 F          NA

Two rows, ids 101 and 103. The test sex == "F" is TRUE on rows 1 and 3, so those stay. The missing weight on row 3 does not matter: the test was on sex, not on weight_kg.

clinic |>
  select(id, weight_kg)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
     id weight_kg
  <dbl>     <dbl>
1   101      61.2
2   102      78.5
3   103      NA

Three rows and two columns. select() keeps every row and the named columns, in the order you named them.

clinic |>
  arrange(desc(weight_kg))
# A tibble: 3 × 3
     id sex   weight_kg
  <dbl> <chr>     <dbl>
1   102 M          78.5
2   101 F          61.2
3   103 F          NA

102 (78.5 kg), then 101 (61.2 kg), then 103. The missing value goes last. arrange() puts missing values at the end whichever direction you sort, so desc() does not bring it to the top.

blocks.prompt:
Read the penguin file.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

How many rows are Chinstrap penguins? The species is written in the file exactly as “Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)”.
blocks.answer:
penguins_raw |>
  filter(Species == "Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)") |>
  nrow()
[1] 68

68 rows are Chinstrap penguins. The test must match the text exactly, letter for letter, including the capital C and the part in brackets.

blocks.prompt:
Read the penguin file.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

How many rows from Biscoe island have a flipper length of 210 mm or more? Give the number with its unit of count and its condition.
blocks.answer:
penguins_raw |>
  filter(Island == "Biscoe", `Flipper Length (mm)` >= 210) |>
  nrow()
[1] 109

109 rows from Biscoe have a flipper length of 210 mm or more. The comma joins the two tests, so both must be TRUE. >= includes a flipper of exactly 210 mm; > would leave it out.

blocks.prompt:
Read the penguin file.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

The two isotope columns are Delta 15 N (o/oo) and Delta 13 C (o/oo). How many rows are missing both? How many are missing at least one?
blocks.answer:
Both missing: join the two tests with &.

penguins_raw |>
  filter(is.na(`Delta 15 N (o/oo)`) & is.na(`Delta 13 C (o/oo)`)) |>
  nrow()
[1] 13

At least one missing: join them with |.

penguins_raw |>
  filter(is.na(`Delta 15 N (o/oo)`) | is.na(`Delta 13 C (o/oo)`)) |>
  nrow()
[1] 14

13 rows are missing both isotope values and 14 are missing at least one. So one row has a carbon value and no nitrogen value. “And” can only give a count the same size as “or” or smaller, never larger.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague wants the number of rows for Adelie penguins and writes:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  filter(Species == "Adelie penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)") |>
  nrow()
[1] 0

They report “there are no Adelie penguins in the file”. Find what broke.
blocks.answer:
The test does not match the text in the file. Look at the values that are there:

penguins_raw |>
  count(Species)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Species                                       n
  <chr>                                     <int>
1 Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)         152
2 Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)    68
3 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)           124

The file writes “Adelie Penguin”, with a capital P. The other two species have a small p. The comparison == works letter for letter. So “penguin” never equals “Penguin”, and the test is FALSE on every row. Copy the value exactly:

penguins_raw |>
  filter(Species == "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)") |>
  nrow()
[1] 152

152 rows are Adelie penguins. (count(), met in section 10, gives the number of rows for each value of a column.)

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: the code ran, the spelling looks right, and 0 is a real number. But a species the study was built around cannot have no rows. An answer of zero is the moment to print the values you tested against.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague wants the rows with no sex recorded and writes:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  filter(Sex == NA) |>
  nrow()
[1] 0

They write in their notes: “sex was recorded for every penguin”. Find what broke, and give the right count.
blocks.answer:
The test Sex == NA is NA on every row. A comparison with an unknown value is unknown. The function filter() drops every row whose test is NA, so it drops all of them. The test must be is.na():

penguins_raw |>
  filter(is.na(Sex)) |>
  nrow()
[1] 11

11 rows have no sex recorded.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: zero missing is a common and welcome result, and nothing on the screen says the test was meaningless. The line reads correctly as English.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague wants the male and female penguins on Dream island and writes:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
penguins_raw |>
  filter(Island == "Dream", Sex == "MALE" | "FEMALE")
Error in `filter()`:
ℹ In argument: `Sex == "MALE" | "FEMALE"`.
Caused by error in `Sex == "MALE" | "FEMALE"`:
! operations are possible only for numeric, logical or complex types

Read the error. Say what broke and fix it.
blocks.answer:
Sex == "MALE" | "FEMALE" is English, not R. R works out Sex == "MALE" first, which gives TRUE or FALSE. Then it tries | between that and the text “FEMALE”. The sign | needs TRUE or FALSE on both sides. A piece of text is neither, so R stops. (The error’s “complex” is a type of number this book does not use.)

Each side of | must be a whole test. Or use %in%, which says the same thing in one go:

penguins_raw |>
  filter(Island == "Dream", Sex %in% c("MALE", "FEMALE")) |>
  nrow()
[1] 123

123 rows on Dream have sex recorded as MALE or FEMALE.

Why the wrong line looks reasonable: it is how you would say it aloud. With numbers instead of text, the same mistake does not stop with an error; it quietly keeps the wrong rows, which is worse.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague wants the mean body mass without the two missing values and writes:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(`Body Mass (g)`))

mean(penguins_raw$`Body Mass (g)`)
# A tibble: 342 × 17
   studyName `Sample Number` Species Region Island Stage `Individual ID`
   <chr>               <dbl> <chr>   <chr>  <chr>  <chr> <chr>
 1 PAL0708                 1 Adelie… Anvers Torge… Adul… N1A1
 2 PAL0708                 2 Adelie… Anvers Torge… Adul… N1A2
 3 PAL0708                 3 Adelie… Anvers Torge… Adul… N2A1
 4 PAL0708                 5 Adelie… Anvers Torge… Adul… N3A1
 5 PAL0708                 6 Adelie… Anvers Torge… Adul… N3A2
 6 PAL0708                 7 Adelie… Anvers Torge… Adul… N4A1
 7 PAL0708                 8 Adelie… Anvers Torge… Adul… N4A2
 8 PAL0708                 9 Adelie… Anvers Torge… Adul… N5A1
 9 PAL0708                10 Adelie… Anvers Torge… Adul… N5A2
10 PAL0708                11 Adelie… Anvers Torge… Adul… N6A1
# ℹ 332 more rows
# ℹ 10 more variables: `Clutch Completion` <chr>, `Date Egg` <date>,
#   `Culmen Length (mm)` <dbl>, `Culmen Depth (mm)` <dbl>,
#   `Flipper Length (mm)` <dbl>, `Body Mass (g)` <dbl>, Sex <chr>,
#   `Delta 15 N (o/oo)` <dbl>, `Delta 13 C (o/oo)` <dbl>,
#   Comments <chr>
[1] NA

The filter() printed 342 rows, so they expected a number. They got NA. Find what broke.
blocks.answer:
The result of filter() was printed and then thrown away. The function never changes penguins_raw. It hands back a new data frame, and nothing gave that one a name. So mean() was given the original column, missing values and all, and a mean with a missing value in it is missing.

Assign the filtered data frame, then take the mean of its column:

weighed <- penguins_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(`Body Mass (g)`))

nrow(weighed)
mean(weighed$`Body Mass (g)`)
[1] 342
[1] 4201.754

342 rows have a body mass, and their mean is about 4202 g (4201.754 as printed).

Why the wrong code looks reasonable: the filter printed the right number of rows, so it looked as if it had done its job. It had. It just did not do it to penguins_raw.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague wants the heaviest penguin in the file and writes:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  arrange(`Body Mass (g)`) |>
  select(Species, `Body Mass (g)`) |>
  print(n = 1)
# A tibble: 344 × 2
  Species                                   `Body Mass (g)`
  <chr>                                               <dbl>
1 Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)            2700
# ℹ 343 more rows

They report “the heaviest penguin was a Chinstrap at 2700 g”. Find what broke.
blocks.answer:
arrange() sorts smallest first. The top row is the lightest penguin, not the heaviest. Wrap the column in desc():

penguins_raw |>
  arrange(desc(`Body Mass (g)`)) |>
  select(Species, `Body Mass (g)`) |>
  print(n = 1)
# A tibble: 344 × 2
  Species                           `Body Mass (g)`
  <chr>                                       <dbl>
1 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)            6300
# ℹ 343 more rows

The heaviest penguin was a Gentoo at 6300 g.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: 2700 g is a real penguin’s mass, and “top row” feels like “top value”. Check a sort by looking at the last row as well as the first, or by asking whether the number is plausible as a maximum.

blocks.prompt: A line in a made-up field report says: “More than half of the Adelie penguins on Torgersen were female.” Check it against the file, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Read the file and keep the Adelie penguins on Torgersen. Then count each value of Sex.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  filter(
    Species == "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)",
    Island == "Torgersen"
  ) |>
  count(Sex)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Sex        n
  <chr>  <int>
1 FEMALE    24
2 MALE      23
3 <NA>       5

52 rows are Adelie penguins on Torgersen: 24 FEMALE, 23 MALE, 5 with no sex recorded.

The claim depends on the denominator.

out of all 52: 24 ÷ 52 = 0.46, so 46%, less than half
out of the 47 with sex recorded: 24 ÷ 47 = 0.51, so 51%, more than half

So “more than half” is true only if the 5 unrecorded rows are left out of the bottom of the fraction. A report should say which denominator it used.

What it does not establish: a share of birds, because one bird can appear in more than one row (section 8). Nor anything about penguins on Torgersen outside this file, or about the 5 rows whose sex is unknown. Counted out of all 52, the FEMALE rows number somewhere from 24 to 29, depending on those 5. They are more than half only if at least 3 of the 5 are female. 26 is exactly half, and 27 ÷ 52 = 0.52.

blocks.prompt: In a made-up lab meeting, someone says: “The Gentoo penguins over 6 kg were all males.” Turn this into code, run it, and say what the result does not establish.
blocks.answer:
6 kg is 6000 g, the unit of the column. Keep Gentoo penguins heavier than 6000 g and look at their sex.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Two Gentoo rows have a body mass over 6000 g, at 6300 g and 6050 g, and both are recorded as male. The sentence is true of this file.

What it does not establish:

  • That heavy Gentoo penguins are male in general. Two rows are two rows.
  • Anything about the Gentoo row with no body mass, N38A2. filter() dropped it, because its test was NA.
  • Anything about a penguin of exactly 6000 g. “Over 6 kg” became > 6000, which leaves 6000 out. If the speaker meant “6 kg or more”, the test is >= 6000. Run that too:
